newsitem.title: UK: Dutch player denies British soccer bribery charges.
newsitem.headline: Dutch player denies British soccer bribery charges.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers told a British soccer bribery trial on Wednesday that large cash deposits he made into a bank account came from business activities in Spain.

Prosecutor David Calvert Smith asked the Dutch-born player why his business partner brought "cash in a suitcase" over from Holland, as Segers had maintained, rather than simply transfer the money into his bank account from Spain or the Netherlands.
"In Spain we dealt with a lot of cash. In Spain they've got a bad reputation as bad payers," Segers said.

Segers, 35, is accused along with former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging soccer games for a Far Eastern gambling syndicate.

The prosecution case against Segers hangs on bank and telephone billing records, showing in particular a series of bunched calls around the dates of matches the defendants are alleged to have thrown and of money transactions.

Segers has told the court on previous days that he was paid money by Lim simply to predict Dutch soccer games or give him information on English teams. Like the other defendants, he has denied the charge of giving or taking money to influence games.
He has described some of the large amounts of money paid into his Swiss bank account as proceeds of the a company in which he is a partner.

The prosecution alleges the venture never generated the large amounts of cash deposited, and Calvert Smith said it was quite unrealistic of Segers to suggest he got paid 1,500 pounds ($2,451) a week simply to forecast the outcome of Dutch games.
Calvert Smith also pointed out that the money from Lim dried up after the Sun newspaper printed a story alleging that Grobbelaar had been taking money to throw games.
Answering questions in a neutral voice, Dutch-born Segers repeatedly said on Wednesday that he could not remember why he phoned Lim or Fashanu at specific times three or more years ago.
But Segers became exasperated at one point when the prosecution alleged the calls related to games he was playing in, and betting by Far Eastern gamblers on these games.
"I don't know what you're trying to get," he told Calvert Smith. "It's phone calls win, lose or draw."
He insisted the calls to Lim, also known as Richard, were simply about forecasting Dutch games. "It's got nothing to do with betting or whatever you're accusing me of." ($1=.6120 Pound)
